Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration:
Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement

Kaixuan Liu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Emory University Affiliation: Atlanta, GA 30322 Email: kaixuan.liu@emory.edu    Guojun Xiong ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: John Hopcroft Center for Computer Science Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Shanghai, China Email: gjxiong@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce IAPO, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO’s deployed plans reach the strongest system’s accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on the two code benchmarks.

Keywords: multi-agent orchestration, policy improvement, interaction effects, certified updates, LLM agents

   

November 5, 2026

1  Introduction

Large language model (LLM)-based agents have achieved strong results in multi-step reasoning (Yao et al., 2022), code generation (Shinn et al., 2023), and tool use (Schick et al., 2023). Organizing several such agents into a multi-agent system extends these capabilities further, as agents that debate (Du et al., 2023), role-play (Li et al., 2023), or converse (Wu et al., 2023) often outperform each of their members on complex tasks. This benefit, however, depends on how the collaboration is organized: which agent acts next, which artifacts it may read, and when the process terminates (Zhang, 2026). What an agent reads also determines how much it influences the others, and hence what a population of interacting agents comes to believe collectively (Liu et al., 2026a).

Early multi-agent systems specify this organization manually through fixed role assignments and communication pipelines (Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023), which limits their transfer across tasks and domains. Subsequent work automates parts of the design: GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) and G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2024) optimize communication topologies, MasRouter (Yue et al., 2025) learns to route queries among agents, and ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b), and MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025a) search over entire workflows. Nevertheless, these methods largely fix the organization before execution and cannot adapt it to the intermediate results produced during a task. More recently, orchestration has been cast as a sequential decision problem, in which a central orchestrator observes the evolving state of a task and is trained by reinforcement learning (RL) to decide how to proceed at every step (Dang et al., 2026; Nielsen et al., 2026). The same principle has been extended to training the coordinated agents jointly with the orchestrator (Liu et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026), producing systems that surpass the strongest individual agents at reduced inference cost (Dang et al., 2026; Nielsen et al., 2026).

Although this paradigm has shown clear empirical gains, its training objectives are inherited directly from single-agent policy optimization (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024), which credits each decision with its own advantage while treating all other decisions in the episode as fixed. This approximation is justified by trust-region arguments that bound its error through the per-step policy divergence (Kakade and Langford, 2002; Schulman et al., 2015), and multi-agent extensions control the error in the same per-step manner (Kuba et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2024). Orchestration violates the premise of these arguments in two ways. First, the decisions within an episode depend on one another, since the effect of each decision on the outcome changes with the decisions made before it. A joint change to several decisions can therefore improve performance even when every single change degrades it, and an objective that adds up per-decision credits cannot detect such joint improvements. Second, an orchestrator makes many decisions in one episode. Even if each decision changes only slightly, the errors add up across decisions, so a per-step trust region no longer keeps the approximation accurate over the length of a whole episode.

To address these challenges, we develop an interaction theory of policy improvement for orchestration and propose IAPO (Interaction-Aware Policy Optimization). We show that the performance difference between two policies is a finite sum of interaction terms among decisions. Each term can be estimated from trajectories without a critic, and the existing objective is the first-order term. This objective has the correct gradient but misses all interactions between organizational decisions, such as which worker to call and which outputs it may read, so any update rule that treats these decisions separately can lose half of the possible gain. We further bound each interaction term by how often the decisions involved are made, which implies that a trust region should limit the policy change weighted by visit counts. Based on this theory, IAPO optimizes the first- and second-order terms in one pass over each trajectory and accepts an update only if a high-confidence lower bound on its gain is positive. We prove that every accepted update improves performance with high probability. On controlled orchestration tasks, IAPO reaches the best possible gain on all three tasks, while the existing objective fails on two, and IAPO never accepts a harmful update. On long-input versions of five benchmarks, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO’s deployed plans reach the strongest system’s accuracy with fewer tokens in every environment and, at that system’s token budget, exceed it significantly on GSM8K, MATH and DROP under at least one cost weight; removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.

  • •

    Exact Interaction Theory: We derive an exact, finite expansion of the performance difference between two orchestration policies, which identifies existing objectives as its single-decision terms and characterizes the omitted interactions through their curvature, visit-count bounds, and sample complexity.

  • •

    Practical Algorithm: We propose IAPO, which jointly optimizes the single-decision and pairwise terms in one pass per trajectory and accepts an update only when its gain is certified with high confidence. Its analysis extends to jointly trained agents.

  • •

    Theoretical and Empirical Validation: We prove that ignoring interactions can forfeit half of the attainable gain and that IAPO accepts only improving updates with high probability, and we confirm on controlled tasks that IAPO recovers gains missed by existing objectives without accepting harmful updates, and on five LLM orchestration benchmarks that it matches or exceeds the strongest of fifteen baselines at lower cost.

2  Problem Formulation

In this section, we formulate multi-agent orchestration as an episodic MDP and define our optimization objective.

2.1  Multi-Agent Orchestration

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a finite set of tasks and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} a finite set of outputs, such as text responses. A task q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} is drawn from a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} and solved by the agents 𝒩={0,1,…,M}\mathcal{N}=\{0,1,\ldots,M\}, where agent 00 is the orchestrator and agents j∈[M]j\in[M] are workers, such as LLMs, tools, and verifiers. The orchestrator solves the task through a sequence of worker calls. Let y1,…,yk∈𝒴y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\in\mathcal{Y} be the outputs of the first kk calls. In the (k+1)(k+1)-th call, the orchestrator chooses a worker j∈[M]j\in[M] and an input set ℰ⊆{y1,…,yk}\mathcal{E}\subseteq\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\} of earlier outputs, and worker jj reads task qq and ℰ\mathcal{E} and returns a new output yk+1∈𝒴y_{k+1}\in\mathcal{Y}. Each call to worker jj costs cj≥0c_{j}\geq 0, and at most KK calls are allowed. Instead of calling a worker, the orchestrator may stop, and the task and the outputs collected so far are scored by a task reward R∈[0,1]R\in[0,1].

2.3  Learning Objective

Our goal is to solve each task with high reward at low cost. We keep the worker policies π1,…,πM\pi^{1},\dots,\pi^{M} fixed and optimize the orchestrator policy π0\pi^{0} to maximize the expected task reward minus the cost of calls:

maxπ0⁡J⁡(π):=𝔼π​[R⁡(q,h)−λ​∑(j,ℰ,y)∈hcj],\max_{\pi^{0}}J(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[R(q,h)-\lambda\sum_{(j,\mathcal{E},y)\in h}c_{j}\Big], (1)

where hh is the interaction history when the episode ends. By the rewards defined in Section 2.2, J⁡(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=1Hrt​(st,at)]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=1}^{H}r_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})] is the expected return of the MDP, so (1) is a standard RL problem in π0\pi^{0}. Our analysis also covers the case where some workers are trained.

3  IAPO

To improve the reward–cost objective (1), IAPO constructs policy updates from an exact interaction expansion (Section 3.1), controls their approximation error (Section 3.2), and certifies their performance using independent data (Section 3.3). Figure 1 gives an overview.

3.1  An Interaction View of Policy Improvement

An orchestrator decision affects subsequent worker outputs, actions, and call costs. To analyze the resulting interactions, let π\pi be the reference policy and π′\pi^{\prime} a candidate that updates only the orchestrator. We impose the following condition to express J⁡(π′)−J⁡(π)J(\pi^{\prime})-J(\pi) using trajectories from π\pi.

For a trajectory sampled from π\pi, define the likelihood ratio ρt=πt′​(at∣st)/πt​(at∣st)\rho_{t}=\pi^{\prime}_{t}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})/\pi_{t}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}). Since worker policies and transitions are fixed, their ratios are 11, and the likelihood ratio of a trajectory prefix through tt is ∏t′=1tρt′\prod_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\rho_{t^{\prime}}. Importance sampling gives the exact improvement in JJ:

Expanding the likelihood-ratio product in (2), with all summation indices ranging over [t][t], gives:

+∑t1<t2<t3(ρt1−1)(ρt2−1)(ρt3−1)\displaystyle+\sum_{t_{1}<t_{2}<t_{3}}(\rho_{t_{1}}-1)(\rho_{t_{2}}-1)(\rho_{t_{3}}-1)
+∑m=4t∑t1<⋯<tm(ρt1−1)⋯(ρtm−1).\displaystyle+\sum_{m=4}^{t}\sum_{t_{1}<\cdots<t_{m}}(\rho_{t_{1}}-1)\cdots(\rho_{t_{m}}-1).

Each factor ρt′−1\rho_{t^{\prime}}-1 represents a decision-level policy change, while products capture interactions across decisions. Rearranging (2) by interaction order and replacing returns by advantages yields the exact decomposition below.

The first-order term J(1)J^{(1)} recovers the advantage-weighted objective underlying PPO-style optimization (Schulman et al., 2017), and higher orders capture the effects of changing several decisions along the same trajectory.

Frozen workers contribute no likelihood-ratio changes, but repeated orchestrator decisions still interact. Their contribution appears in policy curvature.

Thus, the first-order objective has the correct local gradient but misses interaction-induced curvature that can affect the quality of finite policy updates.

3.2  Interaction-Aware Policy Optimization

Since bb is fixed before validation, these bounds apply conditionally on training. For either statistic ZZ, let Z¯\bar{Z} and σ^Z\hat{\sigma}_{Z} be its validation mean and sample standard deviation, and BZ,ηB_{Z,\eta} its absolute bound. The empirical Bernstein inequality (Maurer and Pontil, 2009) gives the confidence radius:

ξη​(Z)=σ^Z​2​log⁡(8​|Λ|/δ)n+14​BZ,η​log⁡(8​|Λ|/δ)3​(n−1).\xi_{\eta}(Z)=\hat{\sigma}_{Z}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(8|\Lambda|/\delta)}{n}}+\frac{14B_{Z,\eta}\log(8|\Lambda|/\delta)}{3(n-1)}. (12)

We take the larger of the two valid lower confidence bounds:

Lη=max⁡{Z¯2−ξη​(Z2)−ϵ⁡(η),Z¯IS−ξη​(ZIS)}.L_{\eta}=\max\big\{\bar{Z}_{2}-\xi_{\eta}(Z_{2})-\epsilon(\eta),\ \bar{Z}_{\mathrm{IS}}-\xi_{\eta}(Z_{\mathrm{IS}})\big\}. (13)

The first accounts for truncation error, while the second uses unbiased importance sampling. Their maximum remains a lower confidence bound on true policy improvement.

IAPO selects the largest positive certificate, retaining π\pi if all certificates are nonpositive. Let π^\hat{\pi} be the selected policy and define:

cη=min⁡{ξη​(Z2)+ϵ⁡(η),ξη​(ZIS)}.c_{\eta}=\min\big\{\xi_{\eta}(Z_{2})+\epsilon(\eta),\xi_{\eta}(Z_{\mathrm{IS}})\big\}.

Across successive rounds κ\kappa, assigning level δ/2κ\delta/2^{\kappa} ensures joint coverage by a union bound. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full update procedure, and the trajectory-level computation is given in Appendix E.3. The betting confidence bound of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2024) can replace (12) (Appendix E.7), and it admits a per-problem baseline (Appendix I.1). Appendix F extends IAPO to policies far from π\pi, which gain only through coordinated changes.

4  Experiments

We evaluate IAPO in two settings. Controlled tasks, whose trajectories can be enumerated exactly, check the theory (Section 4.5). Orchestration over LLM workers on five long-input benchmarks compares accuracy and cost with published systems and ablates the interaction term (Sections 4.1 to 4.4).

4.1  Setup

Environments.

We build long-input versions of GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021). A problem’s own unit (its statements, passage or function specification) is placed among 30 to 90 units of other problems, so one worker reading everything is not already as good as any team. A document holds 81, 91, 31, 61 and 61 units, and the test splits have 790, 220, 800, 333 and 131 problems (Appendix H). These are our own constructions, not the standard benchmarks, so absolute accuracies are not comparable with published numbers on the originals; every system is evaluated on the same constructed inputs. Every system receives the same question text, which includes the opening words of the target unit. The baselines also read the whole document; the orchestrated team reaches it only through an evidence finder, whose BM25 retriever the baselines lack, or a generalist that reads all of it. All workers are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) served by vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) at temperature 1, following the protocol of MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025a).

Orchestration task.

At each of at most five decisions (four on code) the orchestrator calls one of eight roles (planner, evidence finder, analyst, second answerer, calculator, checker, selector) or stops; code adds MaAS’s test-and-repair operator. It observes an embedding of the task and a few state flags, never a score. The reward is accuracy minus λ\lambda times tokens per 32,76832{,}768. We train with λ=0.076\lambda{=}0.076, the protocol’s value (IAPO), and with λ=1\lambda{=}1, which trades accuracy for tokens (IAPO-Lite). Our trajectories are capped at 32,76832{,}768 tokens; the baselines, which read the whole document, run with 131,072131{,}072 or 393,216393{,}216 tokens.

Training and certification.

IAPO runs one round from the uniform policy. It fits one bounded update for each step in Λ={0.25,0.5,1}\Lambda{=}\{0.25,0.5,1\} on 6,4006{,}400 proposal episodes (200200 training problems, 3232 repeats each), adds three certified leaps (Appendix F.1), and certifies every candidate with betting bounds at total level δ=0.05\delta{=}0.05 on 8,0008{,}000 validation episodes drawn from the remaining training problems. Test problems are never used for fitting or selection. The certificate covers net return on the validation distribution, so test accuracy is an empirical question. Search and training tokens are excluded from the per-problem costs; one MBPP run uses about 1.7×1081.7\times 10^{8} in total (Appendix I). Each configuration is trained twice (three times for MATH, IAPO), results are averaged over runs, and all rules were fixed before the runs.

Evaluation.

Each test problem is run four times, and we report accuracy and tokens per problem for one episode. Since the baselines spend more tokens, we also evaluate at matched budget: a majority vote (on code, MaAS’s selector over programs, with its tokens counted) over the most episodes whose tokens fit the strongest baseline’s. The number of episodes never depends on accuracy. Differences are paired by problem and called significant when z>2z>2 (Appendix I).

Baselines.

We run fifteen published systems on the same executor and splits, each as released, so none has a retriever. The single-agent group is CoT (Wei et al., 2022), ComplexCoT (Fu et al., 2023) and self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023). The hand-crafted multi-agent group is MultiPersona (Wang et al., 2024), LLM-Debate (Du et al., 2023), LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023), DyLAN (Liu et al., 2023), AgentVerse (Chen et al., 2023) and MacNet (Qian et al., 2025). The automated group is AutoAgents (Chen et al., 2024), GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b), MAS-Zero (Ke et al., 2025) and MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025a). Not every system runs on every benchmark, and Appendix H lists the setup of each.

4.2  Accuracy and Cost

Accuracy at matched compute.

At the strongest baseline’s budget (Table 1), IAPO leads by 2.32.3 points on GSM8K, 3.63.6 on DROP and 9.79.7 on MBPP (z=6.3z{=}6.3, against DyLAN), and is level with the strongest baseline on MATH (+0.3+0.3) and HumanEval (+0.5+0.5). The GSM8K and DROP differences are significant (Appendix J). IAPO-Lite, trained with the higher token price, goes further on GSM8K (+5.6+5.6), MATH (+6.0+6.0, z=2.6z{=}2.6) and MBPP (+7.2+7.2, z=4.6z{=}4.6), and gives up accuracy on DROP (−4.5-4.5) and HumanEval (−8.1-8.1) in exchange for fewer tokens.

Cost.

One deployed IAPO episode costs 5.1k to 11.5k tokens, against 26.5k to 121.9k for the strongest baselines, that is 2.7 to 24 times fewer (Figure 2); IAPO-Lite costs 1.0k to 5.6k. On code a single episode already matches or beats the strongest baseline: 81.1% on MBPP at 5.1k tokens against DyLAN’s 71.2% at 121.9k, and 83.7% on HumanEval at 9.9k against MaAS’s 83.8% at 26.5k. The matched-budget plans spend 20.4k to 50.8k tokens per problem, each within the strongest baseline’s budget.

4.3  Ablation on the Interaction Term

The first-order variant removes J(2)J^{(2)} from fitting and plan ranking; validation, certification, retriever and roles are the same, so its gap to IAPO comes from the interaction term alone. For IAPO, the interaction term raises accuracy by 17.317.3 points on MBPP and 7.27.2 on HumanEval (both z>2z{>}2), by 1.41.4 on DROP and 0.60.6 on GSM8K, and leaves MATH unchanged, while IAPO uses 32%32\% to 58%58\% of the first-order variant’s tokens on every benchmark (Figure 3). For IAPO-Lite it raises accuracy by 13.013.0 points on GSM8K, 12.912.9 on HumanEval, 2.92.9 on MBPP and 2.72.7 on MATH (all z>2z{>}2) and lowers it by 0.50.5 on DROP, where its tokens rise to 125%125\%. The paired differences and zz-values are in Appendix J.

4.4  What the Policies Deploy

The deployed plans show where the interaction term pays (Appendix J). Test-and-repair helps only after a program exists, a pair of decisions. IAPO deploys it in all four code runs; the first-order variant never proposes it, fills the slots with a second programmer, and loses 1717 points on MBPP and 77 on HumanEval at 3.13.1 and 1.81.8 times the tokens. On question answering and mathematics, all seven IAPO runs follow the evidence finder with the analyst, usually with a checker and the second answerer after it, while the first-order variant never calls the analyst and reads the whole document with the second answerer instead. The analyst alone loses points on every benchmark, so a first-order score never selects it, yet following the evidence finder with the analyst gains (Appendix J).

4.5  Controlled Tasks

One probability qq is shared by NN decisions with frozen binary workers, and all 2N2^{N} trajectories are enumerated (Appendix G). Complementarity is the trap of Proposition E.7, Redundancy has substitutes, and Evidence threshold has N=6N{=}6.

The first-order score is zero for every step on Complementarity (oracle gain 0.1480.148) and overshoots on Redundancy (0.0060.006 against 0.0100.010), while the second-order score picks the oracle step on both. On Evidence threshold the truncation bound exceeds the second-order gain, so Z2Z_{2} alone deploys a gain of 0.0870.087, and adding ZISZ_{\mathrm{IS}} restores 0.3560.356. Across 6,0006{,}000 validation runs, no candidate with negative gain was accepted.

Appendix A Assumptions, Conventions, and Notation

Throughout, π\pi is the current policy, which generates the data, π′\pi^{\prime} is a candidate policy, 𝔼π\mathbb{E}_{\pi} and Prπ\Pr_{\pi} are over trajectories of π\pi, and all other quantities are as in Sections 2 and 3.

A.1  The Overlap Assumption

Assumption 3.1 (Overlap). There exists W≥1W\geq 1 such that πt′​(a∣s)≤W​πt​(a∣s)\pi^{\prime}_{t}(a\mid s)\leq W\pi_{t}(a\mid s) for every t∈[H]t\in[H], every state ss reachable under π\pi, and every a∈𝒜⁡(s)a\in\mathcal{A}(s).

By Lemma B.3, Assumption 3.1 gives Prπ′⁡(τt)>0⇒Prπ⁡(τt)>0\Pr_{\pi^{\prime}}(\tau_{t})>0\Rightarrow\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{t})>0, and ρt′≤W\rho_{t^{\prime}}\leq W gives ∏t′≤tρt′≤Wt\prod_{t^{\prime}\leq t}\rho_{t^{\prime}}\leq W^{t}. Moreover:

  • •

    WW enters only the estimators, through ρt∈[0,W]\rho_{t}\in[0,W]; the expansion of Theorem 3.2 is an identity for every π′\pi^{\prime}, and overlap only writes each term as an expectation under π\pi (Remark B.8).

  • •

    The bounded update (7) satisfies Assumption 3.1 with W=1+ηW=1+\eta (Proposition 3.5); PPO clipping bounds ρt\rho_{t} only on the sampled actions and does not imply Assumption 3.1 for the returned policy.

    For estimation the assumption cannot be dropped: πt′​(a∣s)>0=πt​(a∣s)\pi^{\prime}_{t}(a\mid s)>0=\pi_{t}(a\mid s) at a reachable ss implies Prπ⁡(st=s,at=a)=0\Pr_{\pi}(s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a)=0, so no number of trajectories of π\pi identifies the reward that π′\pi^{\prime} collects after (s,a)(s,a).

A.2  Conventions

Finite trajectories.

|𝒬|,|𝒴|,H<∞|\mathcal{Q}|,|\mathcal{Y}|,H<\infty, so all state, action, and trajectory sets are finite, every expectation below is a finite sum, and sums, expectations, and derivatives commute.

Fixed horizon.

An episode that stops before step HH stays until step HH in an absorbing state with a single action and zero reward, attributed to no agent in 𝒩\mathcal{N}. There ρt=1\rho_{t}=1, so these steps enter no term below and no visit count. With at most KK calls of two steps each and one stop, H=2​K+1H=2K+1 and the orchestrator acts at most K+1K+1 times.

The state determines the history.

Let τt≔(s1,a1,…,st,at)\tau_{t}\coloneqq(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,s_{t},a_{t}) for t≥1t\geq 1 and τ0\tau_{0} be empty. An orchestrator state (q,hk)(q,h_{k}) and a worker state (q,hk,j,ℰ)(q,h_{k},j,\mathcal{E}) record the task, the earlier calls (jℓ,ℰℓ,yℓ)(j_{\ell},\mathcal{E}_{\ell},y_{\ell}), and the current call, which are the earlier actions; the earlier states are functions of these, so sts_{t} determines τt−1\tau_{t-1}. The proofs use only this property and hold for every finite-horizon MDP that has it.

Acting agents.

At every non-absorbing step, it=i⁡(st)i_{t}=i(s_{t}) and πt​(a∣s)=πi⁡(s)​(a∣s)\pi_{t}(a\mid s)=\pi^{i(s)}(a\mid s). A worker policy πj(⋅∣q,ℰ)\pi^{j}(\cdot\mid q,\mathcal{E}) depends on ss only through (q,ℰ)(q,\mathcal{E}), a function of ss, so we write it as πt(⋅∣s)\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid s).

Reward bounds.

Let r¯t,G¯≥0\bar{r}_{t},\bar{G}\geq 0 satisfy |rt​(s,a)|≤r¯t|r_{t}(s,a)|\leq\bar{r}_{t} for all (s,a)(s,a) and ∑t=1H|rt​(st,at)|≤G¯\sum_{t=1}^{H}|r_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})|\leq\bar{G} on every trajectory. In the orchestration MDP, a trajectory has at most KK calls, each with reward −λ​cj-\lambda c_{j}, and one stop, with reward R∈[0,1]R\in[0,1], so:

∑t=1H|rt​(st,at)|≤λ​∑callscj+R≤λ​K​maxj​cj+1.\sum_{t=1}^{H}|r_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})|\leq\lambda\sum_{\text{calls}}c_{j}+R\leq\lambda K\max_{j}c_{j}+1.

Hence G¯=1+λ​K​maxj​cj\bar{G}=1+\lambda K\max_{j}c_{j} and r¯t=max⁡{1,λ​maxj​cj}\bar{r}_{t}=\max\{1,\lambda\max_{j}c_{j}\} are valid.

Proof.

On any trajectory of π\pi, at most rr steps belong to changed agents, so |S|>r|S|>r implies that some t′∈St^{\prime}\in S has π′it′=πit′\pi^{\prime i_{t^{\prime}}}=\pi^{i_{t^{\prime}}}, hence ρt′=1\rho_{t^{\prime}}=1 and ∏t∈S(ρt−1)=0\prod_{t\in S}(\rho_{t}-1)=0. For a statistic |Z|≤B|Z|\leq B with validation values Y1,…,YnY_{1},\dots,Y_{n}, a finite set F⊂(0,1]F\subset(0,1] of bet sizes, and z∈(−B,B]z\in(-B,B], define:

𝒲⁡(z)≔1|F|​∑ν∈F∏ℓ=1n(1+ν⁡(Yℓ+Bz+B−1)),\mathcal{W}(z)\coloneqq\frac{1}{|F|}\sum_{\nu\in F}\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}\Big(1+\nu\Big(\frac{Y_{\ell}+B}{z+B}-1\Big)\Big),

Appendix G Controlled Experiments

Each controlled task shares one probability qq over NN decisions with frozen binary workers, and the reward arrives at the end: Complementarity (N=2N{=}2, p=1/3p{=}1/3, reward 3​x0​x1−x0−x13x_{0}x_{1}-x_{0}-x_{1}), Redundancy (N=2N{=}2, p=0.2p{=}0.2, reward −x0​x1+0.3​(x0+x1)-x_{0}x_{1}+0.3(x_{0}+x_{1})) and Evidence threshold (N=6N{=}6, p=0.3p{=}0.3, reward 𝟏{∑txt≥3}−0.05∑txt\mathbf{1}\{\sum_{t}x_{t}\geq 3\}-0.05\sum_{t}x_{t}). A candidate with step s∈[−1,1]s\in[-1,1] plays q=p+s​p​(1−p)q=p+s\,p(1-p), which is (7) with η=|s|\eta=|s|, and all 2N2^{N} trajectories are enumerated, with 500 repetitions at δ=0.05\delta=0.05. On Complementarity the linear term vanishes at p=13p=\tfrac{1}{3} and a step gains 4​s2/274s^{2}/27, so the first-order score keeps the reference while the second-order score reaches 0.1480.148. On Redundancy a step gains 0.032​s−0.0256​s20.032s-0.0256s^{2}: the first-order score takes s=1s=1 and gains 0.00640.0064, whereas the second-order score takes s=12s=\tfrac{1}{2} on the grid and gains 0.00960.0096. On Evidence threshold the truncation bound ϵ=1.728\epsilon=1.728 exceeds the second-order gain 0.4230.423 at s=1s=1, so the order-two certificate rejects that step at every sample size and accepts only a smaller one (gain 0.0870.087); the importance-sampling certificate accepts the oracle step from n=4096n=4096 (gain 0.3560.356). Across the 6,000 validation runs, no candidate with negative gain was accepted.

Appendix H Environments, Roles and Protocol

Benchmarks.

Each problem is stored as a target unit and a question in AFlow’s format (Zhang et al., 2025b). Its long input shuffles the target unit among DD units of other problems of the same split, using a generator seeded by a hash of the problem text, so that the document is a fixed function of the problem. Units stay whole and numbered, which is what the evidence finder retrieves. The setting follows GSM-IC (Shi et al., 2023), carried to document length. The baselines read the whole document, and the team reaches it only through the evidence finder or the generalist; both receive the same question text, including the opening words of the target unit.

Training problems come from the official training splits and test problems from AFlow’s test splits. GSM8K uses the first 2,000 official training problems in SHA-256 order and 800 of AFlow’s 1,055 test problems (790 with a statement before the question). MATH uses 1,131 official level 4 to 5 problems of MaAS’s four subjects (Zhang et al., 2025a) and 336 test problems (220 with at least two sentences). Because AFlow’s DROP training split has only 200 questions, IAPO trains on 1,000 questions of the official split whose passages are disjoint from AFlow’s splits. MBPP keeps the 333 test problems whose first assertion names the function. HumanEval has no training split, so IAPO trains on 577 problems, AFlow’s 33 validation problems and 544 MBPP problems rewritten as HumanEval prompts (Cassano et al., 2023); none of the test problems is in this training pool.

MATH answers are scored by a matcher that takes the last balanced \boxed{...} from prediction and reference and applies MaAS’s MATH equality (identical strings, numbers within 10−310^{-3}, or a SymPy difference that simplifies to zero). It replaced a matcher that misread some answers, and every MATH arm was rerun with it.

Roles.

Question answering and mathematics use eight roles and code adds Test (Table 3). Teams run in a pipeline regime with typed interfaces: a worker’s product reaches only its designated consumer at the next decision, and candidates are combined only when the selector is chosen. The evidence finder ranks the numbered units with BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009), and Test is MaAS’s public-test operator as released, with up to three repairs. Which roles are legal depends on the decision index and a few flags, and at the last decision only stopping is legal, which leaves 2,016 open-loop plans at five decisions and 432 at four. The orchestrator observes a MiniLM embedding of the task, the role signals, the previous action, the position and the share of the token budget spent, but never a score.

Protocol.

Every call is a chat completion of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in bfloat16 on vLLM, one engine per H200, with a 24,576-token context window, at most 4,096 completion tokens and temperature 1, and both arms run through one metered environment that follows MaAS’s protocol. Tokens are the prompt and completion tokens of every request, retries included. IAPO’s trajectories are capped at 32,76832{,}768 tokens and the baselines’ at 131,072131{,}072 unless Appendix H says otherwise. A trajectory that exhausts its budget or fails with known usage scores 00 at its paid cost, as in MaAS’s evaluator; this happened only on MBPP among IAPO’s test runs (at most 3 of 1,332 episodes per run). The reward is s−λ​N/32,768s-\lambda N/32{,}768 for score ss and NN tokens, with λ=0.076\lambda=0.076 (config A, IAPO), a value fixed in an early pilot so that one extra revision step of about 1,500 tokens breaks even, or λ=1\lambda=1 (CW1, IAPO-Lite).

Baselines.

Table 4 lists how each system was run.

Each system runs as released, adapted only where the shared protocol or the 7B executor forces it, and is then frozen. Systems that search or train read only the benchmark’s training split (MBPP’s for HumanEval), and their search cost is not counted in tokens per problem. On DROP the baselines’ training file, AFlow’s validation split, shares 120 of its 161 passages with the test split. For LLM-Blender both the fused output and the top-ranked candidate are kept and the higher is reported. MaAS’s solving prompt for MATH reaches the model with \boxed as a backspace and “oxed”, so prompting baselines on MATH run with the backslash restored. The strongest baseline of each environment received a second seed where one was run (Debate on GSM8K and DROP, DyLAN on MATH and MBPP, LLM-Blender on DROP and HumanEval, the benchmarks where it was the strongest).

Appendix I IAPO Settings, Certificates and Statistics

All 42 IAPO runs (21 pairs of IAPO and its first-order variant) share the settings of Table 5 within each environment family, apart from the draw salt and the interaction switch.

I.1  Certificates

With three steps and three leaps there are M=9M=9 statistics per run, each at level δ1/9≈2.8×10−3\delta_{1}/9\approx 2.8\times 10^{-3} for δ1=0.025\delta_{1}=0.025. A step is certified by Lη=max⁡{L⁡(Z2)−ϵ⁡(η),L⁡(ZIS)}L_{\eta}=\max\{L(Z_{2})-\epsilon(\eta),L(Z_{\mathrm{IS}})\} with the betting bound of Appendix E.7, found by 48 bisection steps and rounded down; the interval lengths and ϵ⁡(η)\epsilon(\eta) are in Table 6. A leap is certified by the betting bound on the paired differences di=G1​(τ~i)−G1​(τi)d_{i}=G_{1}(\tilde{\tau}_{i})-G_{1}(\tau_{i}) for i≤4,000i\leq 4{,}000, where τ~i\tilde{\tau}_{i} starts from the problem of validation draw τi\tau_{i} with its own seeds. The deployed policy is the reference, step or leap with the largest certificate, and a candidate with a positive certificate was deployed in all 42 runs. One MBPP run spends about 2.9×1072.9\times 10^{7} tokens on proposal trajectories, 3.6×1073.6\times 10^{7} on validation and 1.07×1081.07\times 10^{8} on the three leaps, about 1.7×1081.7\times 10^{8} in total, which Table 1 does not include.

Per-problem baseline.

A constant baseline removes the mean return but not the spread between problems, so in validation trajectory ii we use bi∈[g−,g+]b_{i}\in[g_{-},g_{+}], the mean return of the earlier validation trajectories on the same problem, or bb if there is none. Because bib_{i} depends only on trajectories 1,…,i−11,\dots,i-1 and the initial state of trajectory ii, and 𝔼π[∏j≤tρj−1∣s1]=𝔼π[ρt−1∣τt−1,st]=0\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\prod_{j\leq t}\rho_{j}-1\mid s_{1}]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\rho_{t}-1\mid\tau_{t-1},s_{t}]=0, the bib_{i} terms have conditional mean zero and each statistic keeps its mean given the earlier trajectories. The payoff then lies in [g−−g+,g+−g−][g_{-}-g_{+},\,g_{+}-g_{-}], which widens the intervals of Lemma E.3. The values are martingale differences rather than i.i.d.; the proof of Proposition E.6 needs only that the conditional mean is at most zz, so it holds with [z−,z+][z_{-},z_{+}] in place of [−B,B][-B,B], whereas the empirical Bernstein bound would need independence. On competition mathematics with a seven-operator workflow this baseline lowers the standard deviation of ZISZ_{\mathrm{IS}} by about a quarter at every step of the grid.

Leaps.

Every declared plan is scored by the proposal statistic at its leap policy, the plan mixed with ε=0.001\varepsilon=0.001 of the reference, as the mean over the 6,4006{,}400 proposal trajectories minus two standard errors. On question answering and mathematics the 50 top-ranked plans each run on 1,0001{,}000 fresh validation draws and the three with the largest mean net return become the leaps; on code the three top-ranked plans become the leaps directly. The certificate never reads the screening draws. The expansion serves here as a proposal heuristic for distant plans, so the remainder bound does not apply to the leap ratios, while their certificates stay valid because they use paired draws of their own.

Matched budget.

The frozen deployed policy is rerun on the test split with a fresh salt and 10 to 200 repeats per problem. On answer tasks a vote takes the most common non-empty answer key over the first KK episodes, with ties to the earliest; on code the episodes split into groups of KK, each reduced to one program by MaAS’s HumanEval-template selector with its tokens added. KK is the largest count whose tokens per vote fit the strongest baseline’s tokens per episode, for every listed seed. The budgets are 28.6k (GSM8K), 53.8k (MATH), 57.1k (DROP) and 26.5k tokens (HumanEval); on MBPP it is 35.4k, below DyLAN’s 121.9k.

Statistics.

Comparisons are paired by problem on the full test split: per-problem differences of arm means give d¯\bar{d}, SE=sd/n\mathrm{SE}=s_{d}/\sqrt{n} and z=d¯/SEz=\bar{d}/\mathrm{SE}, called significant when z>2z>2. The ablation is scored on net return s−λ​tokens/32,768s-\lambda\,\text{tokens}/32{,}768 with each configuration’s own λ\lambda. An arm’s score is averaged over its runs per problem before the differences are taken, and no run of a reported configuration is left out.

Appendix J Full Results

Table 7 gives one episode of each deployed policy and Table 8 the paired comparisons. Against every baseline, IAPO’s single-episode accuracy on MBPP is higher by at least 8.8 points (best baseline DyLAN, 72.3%), and on HumanEval, apart from MaAS (83.8%), by at least 8.1 points (next best Debate, 75.6%).
